The chat list becomes an ordinary macOS sidebar: chats gathered into sections, search at the top, and rows set closer together. Like Mail and Notes — and less like a phone.

Anyone without a picture of their own gets a little creature instead — their own, and the same one every time. It is drawn here on the device; nothing is sent anywhere. Groups get a cluster of the people in them rather than a letter.
Everybody gets a creature, including the people who did set a picture. Their photographs are not fetched at all.

A made-up account instead of yours, with chats, photos, voice messages and even an invitation already in it. The server lives inside the app and never goes online. Your own account stays where it is: turn this off and you are back in it.
Traffic reaches the server through a bridge instead of going there directly. This is for places where the server cannot be reached.

That is a secret key. The public one is wanted here — the one that starts with npub.

This is where the app and the bridge find each other. Several is not a spare tyre: a request goes out to all of them at once and the answer comes back from whichever was quickest. Leave it empty for the default three.
If the bridge is a closed one, add this key to its ALLOWED_PUBKEYS — otherwise it will not hear you at all.

Every request goes the long way round through a relay and costs 200–350 ms, so signing in and opening chats for the first time are noticeably slower than a direct connection — a second where it used to be instant. New messages, though, arrive almost as fast as they do directly. Large attachments will get through too, but they are better kept off public relays: for media, give the bridge a relay of its own.

Only which server you connect to, when, and how many bytes. The app encrypts the connection to the server itself, so your token, your rooms and your messages — even in unencrypted chats — are hidden from the bridge. Your IP address is seen by the relays, not the bridge.
The app will ask for Face ID, Touch ID, or your device passcode when you come back.

Your conversations are kept on the server in a backup, encrypted. With your recovery code you can read them on any new device.

Until this device is verified, your account has no way to know it is really you — and your older conversations will not come through to it. You can verify it from a phone or computer where you are already signed in.
The app on your other device has to be open right now, or the request will not reach it.
This device has just signed in to your account and is asking you to verify it. If that was you, agree — and then compare the emoji. If it wasn\'t, refuse: somebody else knows your password.
The two devices are working it out between them. The emoji are about to appear on both screens.

Your account trusts this device now. Your older conversations will appear here on their own.
If the emoji really did not match, do not trust this connection, and try again. It may also be that you simply started the verification twice.
That device was given no access to your conversations. But if the sign-in wasn\'t yours, then somebody else knows your password — and it needs changing right now.

That’s all right. Confirm this device from a phone or computer where you’re already signed in, and we’ll give you a new code to replace the lost one.
Without the code and without another device, your old messages can’t come back — they stay encrypted for good. New messages will arrive as usual, and we’ll give you a new recovery code.
Your account password has nothing to do with this: it opens your account, not your old messages.

Not sure which server to choose?
Matrix is an open way for messaging apps to talk to each other. Iskra is one of those apps. There are others, and they all understand each other.

Your account lives on one server, and you can write to people on any other. Email works the same way: you’re on Gmail, your friend is on Yahoo, and the mail still arrives. A Matrix address looks like this: @name:server.

Matrix isn’t owned by one company that could shut it down, sell your data or change the rules. There are thousands of servers, run by foundations, communities and ordinary people. You can run one too.
Messages are encrypted right on your device, and only the person you’re writing to can decrypt them. The server stores and passes them along, but it can’t read them.
Your account lives on one server, and you can write to people on any other — just like email. On every server below you can create an account right in Iskra.
The largest Matrix server, run by the foundation that develops Matrix itself.
One of the oldest community servers. Its owner runs other free services too.
An open server for everyday conversation, free for everyone.
Run by the adminForge team, who host other free services too. Has bridges to other messengers.
You can run a server of your own — then your conversations are entirely in your hands. You’ll need a domain and a little time.
What someone who joins later will see of what was already said. In a protected chat older messages may not open for them: they don’t have the keys.
The address is how the chat is found and opened from a link. Clear it and the chat has none.

Folders gather chats by rules — personal, groups, unread — and sit as tabs above the list. They’re the same on all your devices.
The chats stay where they are — only the tab goes.
Ticked, the chat is in the folder even if it doesn’t fit the rules. Unticked, it never is.
Chats that fit its rules will appear here.
The notification’s title shows which of your accounts it came to.
A message’s menu gets “View JSON” — the event as the server sent it. Useful when a message shows up wrong.
The address the app really talks to — found from the account’s name, not necessarily what was typed at sign-in. A bridge doesn’t change it; it only carries the connection.
Chats also show the events the app normally leaves out — permissions, join rules, calls, picture changes, anything that failed to parse — as a grey line with the type and the sender.
